Repo: /home/lane/MythosMini — a 1,050,241-param byte-level (vocab 257) looped-shared-block transformer trained on fineweb-edu, benchmarked on WikiText-2 byte PPL, BLiMP, ARC-Easy against the Tiny-ML leaderboard (overall = mean of blimp, arc, normalized wiki score; efficiency = overall/log10(params+1) so PARAMETER GROWTH IS PENALIZED only logarithmically — doubling params costs ~5% efficiency but any overall gain counts fully). Current pipeline: procedural Dyck warmup -> 2B-token training (NAdamW, WSD schedule) -> 3-round recursive STM -> benchmark all checkpoints -> SLERP tournament -> SFT instruct phase -> instruct SLERP. Architecture: 4 prelude + 1 shared block looped 2-6x with per-loop LoRA + 4 coda, dim 96, RMSNorm/RoPE/SwiGLU, tied embeddings, DSA-style sparse attention (shared model-level lightning indexer, top-128 keys, 64 local window, FlexAttention short path, chunked long path, 1M max context), FP4 E2M1 QAT on all linears. Recent regression: moving the indexer from per-attention to one shared model-level indexer + detaching the indexer bias for prelude/coda blocks raised throughput 0.85->1.19 Mtok/s but the verification run scored 59.47 overall vs 60.40 before, AND its STM round 3 NaN-diverged (prior runs round 3 gave +0.57; NaN also seen once before with output-embedding centering). All-time best: 60.41 (recursive STM, commit accd37b). GPU: one RTX 5090 32GB, torch 2.10.0+cu128. Known: full-model torch.compile broken (inductor dtype bug + flex recompile issues), STM phase runs at only ~76 ktok/s vs training 1.19 Mtok/s. USER GOAL: push output quality as far as possible toward Gemma-class coherence (text in/text out) — ambition is the point; consider parameter growth, distillation, synthetic data, anything that fits one 5090.

Research via web search: the single most documented path to coherent tiny models is DATA: TinyStories (arXiv 2305.07759) showed 1-10M models produce fluent coherent text when trained on simple synthetic stories. Research: (1) TinyStories and successors — exact data recipes, model sizes, documented quality; (2) knowledge distillation from open teachers (Qwen3-0.6B, SmolLM2-135M/360M, Gemma-3-270M) into a BYTE-LEVEL student (vocab 257) — vocabulary-mismatch distillation (universal logit distillation, synthetic-text generation instead of logit matching); (3) BabyLM challenge winners 2023-2025 exact recipes at 10-100M words; (4) feasibility: generating 100M-1B tokens of TinyStories-style text with a small teacher on one RTX 5090 via vLLM — tokens/hour estimates; or existing open datasets (TinyStories on HF, SmolTalk, Cosmopedia) we could mix in DIRECTLY without generating. CAVEAT to weigh: our benchmarks are WikiText-2 byte PPL + BLiMP + ARC-Easy — would simple-English synthetic data hurt wiki PPL while helping BLiMP/coherence? Concrete, implementable findings only.

TinyStories is a synthetic dataset of short stories that only contain words that a typical 3 to 4-year-olds usually understand, generated by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.

TinyStories can be used to train and evaluate language models that are much smaller than the state-of-the-art models (below 10 million total parameters), or have much simpler architectures (with only one transformer block), yet still produce fluent and consistent stories with several paragraphs that are diverse and have almost perfect grammar, and demonstrate reasoning capabilities.

Universal Logit Distillation (ULD) loss is grounded in optimal transport to address the limitation that logit-based methods typically require teacher and student models to share the same tokenizer. ## Cross-Tokenizer Distillation Approaches

Prior work has approached cross-tokenizer distillation by applying optimal transport to align teacher and student logits, thereby providing vocabulary-agnostic supervision. A complementary approach reduces distributional divergence by approximating marginalized probabilities through sequence alignment.

Several related methods have emerged:

- ULD measures token-wise optimal transport distance between the logits of the student and teacher models, eliminating the dependency on dimensional correspondence

- Multi-Level OT uses optimal transport at both token and sequence levels to preserve local and global logit structure

- A method for enhancing cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation with contextual dynamical mapping was introduced in 2025

# Cross-Tokenizer LLM Distillation via Byte-Level Interface

## Core Method

The paper proposes Byte-Level Distillation (BLD), which enables knowledge transfer between models with different tokenizers by operating at a shared byte-level interface rather than competing token vocabularies.

**Key steps:**
1. Convert teacher's token-level probabilities to byte-level using an approximation algorithm
2. Attach a lightweight byte-level decoder head (10 parallel linear projections) to the student model
3. Distill via KL divergence at the byte level, combined with next-byte and next-token cross-entropy losses
4. Remove the byte-level head after training, leaving a standard token-level model

The authors explain: "we convert the teacher's output distribution to byte-level probabilities, attach a lightweight byte-level decoder head to the student, and distill through this shared byte-level interface."

## Experimental Setup

**Models tested:**
- Llama 3.2 3B (teacher/source) → Qwen2 tokenizer (BPE-to-BPE transfer)
- Llama 3.2 3B → byte-level tokenization (BPE-to-byte transfer)
- OpenMath2-Llama3.1 8B → Gemma2 2B (cross-model distillation)

**Training:** LoRA fine-tuning (rank 64) on Tulu-3 SFT mixture; 5 epochs, batch size 2

## Results vs. Baselines

**BPE-to-BPE transfer** (Table 1):
- BLD achieved highest on PiQA (75.68) and AGI-ZH (35.97)
- ALM + SFT led on 4/7 benchmarks
- All methods struggled with IFEval instruction following

**Cross-tokenizer distillation** (Table 3):
- BLD: GSM8K 62.55 (vs. SFT 59.29, ALM+SFT 61.56)
- SFT led on MATH (22.40 vs. BLD's 20.08)
- Large gap to teacher (87.26 GSM8K)

**Key finding:** "no method, including ours, achieves consistent improvements across all benchmarks," suggesting CTD remains unsolved.

## Code Release

The paper does not mention code availability.

## Overview

The winner of both the Strict and Strict-Small tracks is GPT-BERT, submitted by Charpentier and Samuel (2024).

## Model Architecture and Approach

The model presents a simple way to merge masked language modeling with causal language modeling, resulting in a model that combines the strengths of both modeling paradigms within a single transformer stack – GPT-BERT can be transparently used like any standard causal or masked language model. The hybrid pretraining outperforms masked-only or causal-only models.

## Training Objectives and Hyperparameters

The research uses two training objectives:
- **Masked Next Token Prediction (MNTP)** - a bidirectional masked language modeling approach
- **Causal Language Modeling** - standard left-to-right language modeling

The paper explores different ratios of these objectives during training. During training they vary both the mask token percentage (linear decay from 30% to 15%), and the sequence length.

## Dataset and Resources

The pretraining process was tested on the BabyLM Challenge 2024. The models, training corpora and code were openly released.

from collections import deque
from collections.abc import Iterator
from typing import Protocol

import torch
from torch import Tensor


class BatchSource(Protocol):
    def next_batch(self, batch_size: int) -> Tensor | None: ...


class SequenceBuffer:
    def __init__(self, chunk_iterator: Iterator[Tensor], device: str) -> None:
        self.chunk_iterator = chunk_iterator
        self.device = device
        self.pending: deque[Tensor] = deque()
        self.exhausted = False

    def refill(self, needed: int) -> None:
        held = sum(chunk.shape[0] for chunk in self.pending)
        while held < needed and not self.exhausted:
            try:
                chunk = next(self.chunk_iterator)
            except StopIteration:
                self.exhausted = True
                return
            self.pending.append(chunk)
            held += chunk.shape[0]

    def next_batch(self, batch_size: int) -> Tensor | None:
        if batch_size < 1:
            raise ValueError(f"batch_size must be positive, got {batch_size}")
        self.refill(batch_size)
        rows: list[Tensor] = []
        remaining = batch_size
        while remaining > 0 and self.pending:
            chunk = self.pending.popleft()
            if chunk.shape[0] > remaining:
                rows.append(chunk[:remaining])
                self.pending.appendleft(chunk[remaining:])
                remaining = 0
            else:
                rows.append(chunk)
                remaining -= chunk.shape[0]
        if remaining > 0:
            return None
        batch = torch.cat(rows, dim=0) if len(rows) > 1 else rows[0]
        return batch.to(self.device, non_blocking=True)

from collections.abc import Iterator
from typing import Any

import torch
from torch import Tensor
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, IterableDataset, get_worker_info

from src.mythosmini.config import FINEWEB_CONFIG, FINEWEB_DATASET, LOADER_CHUNK_SEQUENCES
from src.mythosmini.data.packing import pack_token_stream, quality_passes


def stream_fineweb_documents(
    quality_percent: float, shard_index: int, shard_count: int
) -> Iterator[str]:
    from datasets import load_dataset

    dataset: Any = load_dataset(FINEWEB_DATASET, name=FINEWEB_CONFIG, split="train", streaming=True)
    if shard_count > 1:
        dataset = dataset.shard(num_shards=shard_count, index=shard_index)
    for record in dataset:
        if quality_passes(int(record["int_score"]), str(record["id"]), quality_percent):
            yield str(record["text"])


class PackedFineweb(IterableDataset[Tensor]):
    def __init__(self, quality_percent: float, seq_len: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.quality_percent = quality_percent
        self.seq_len = seq_len

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[Tensor]:
        worker = get_worker_info()
        shard_index = worker.id if worker is not None else 0
        shard_count = worker.num_workers if worker is not None else 1
        documents = stream_fineweb_documents(self.quality_percent, shard_index, shard_count)
        return pack_token_stream(documents, self.seq_len)


def build_dataloader(quality_percent: float, seq_len: int, num_workers: int) -> DataLoader[Tensor]:

# BERTtime Stories: Synthetic Data Impact on BabyLM Pretraining

## Setup Details

The researchers trained GPT-Neo models on TinyStories data (5-100M words), then generated continuations to existing stories using nucleus sampling. Their final training combined three components:

- **Original BabyLM corpus** (𝒟baby): 5-50M words
- **TinyStories sample** (𝒟tiny): 5-50M words  
- **Model-generated data** (𝒟gen): Variable amounts from greedy and nucleus sampling (p=0.95)

They trained LTG-BERT encoders on these mixed datasets and evaluated on BLiMP, GLUE, and EWoK benchmarks.

## Key Results

**100M Strict Track:**
- BabyLM baseline only: 69.2 BLiMP, 68.4 GLUE, 65.6 EWoK (avg: 64.0)
- TinyStories (50M) + BabyLM (50M) + Generated (greedy, ~50M extra): 66.6 BLiMP, 71.8 GLUE, 65.0 EWoK (avg: 66.7)
- TinyStories (50M) + BabyLM (50M) + Generated (nucleus-1, ~50M extra): 65.6 BLiMP, 72.7 GLUE, 64.6 EWoK (avg: 67.0)

**10M Strict-Small Track:**
- BabyLM baseline: 60.6 BLiMP, 60.3 GLUE, 57.7 avg
- TinyStories (5M) + BabyLM (5M) + Generated (~5M): 62.6 BLiMP, 71.2 GLUE, 65.3 avg

## Conclusion

Synthetic data provision delivered "mixed results." In the 100M track, GLUE scores improved modestly (68.4→72.7), while BLiMP scores declined slightly. The 10M track showed clearer benefits with larger average improvements.

# Data Composition Study: Results Summary

## Datasets Tested
The researchers evaluated four data sources, all limited to **10 million words**:
- CHILDES (child-directed speech)
- Gutenberg (classic books)
- TinyStories (synthetic simplified stories)
- Mix (diverse combination - the default BabyLM dataset)

## Model Sizes Evaluated
GPT2 variants: 18M, 44M, 97M, and 705M parameters
LLaMA variants: 20M and 360M parameters

## Key BLiMP Results (Filtered metric)

**Smaller models (18M-44M parameters):** Mix performed best
- GPT2-18M on Mix: **63.7**
- GPT2-44M on Mix: **65.6**

**Larger models (97M+ parameters):** Gutenberg excelled
- GPT2-97M on Gutenberg: **65.3**
- GPT2-705M on Gutenberg: **66.8**
- LLaMA-360M on Gutenberg: **66.5**

## Worst Performer

I found comprehensive information about the MiniCPM WSD learning rate scheduler and its training strategy. Here's what the search revealed:

## MiniCPM Training Stages with WSD Scheduler

The overall training of MiniCPM base model includes three stages: stable training stage, decay stage, SFT stage.

### Decay Stage Strategy

In the decay stage, a mixture of the pretraining data and high-quality SFT data is used, with exponential annealing employed for the WSD scheduler. The exponential annealing formula is f(s - T) = 0.5^((s-S)/T), with T set to be 5000 steps (20B tokens).

### Learning Rate Gains from Decay Stage

In MiniCPM, 10% decay completes convergence and enables mixing new data (domain adaptation or SFT) strictly during the decay phase. The WSD scheduler enables efficient convergence by achieving rapid loss reduction in the final decay stage using only 10% of total tokens, and is particularly effective when high-quality data is introduced mid-training.

### Data Mixing Benefits

Due to the pronounced loss decrease observed during the decay stage of the WSD LRS, integrating high-quality labeled data in this phase presents dual advantages, fostering more comprehensive model learning. The data mixture can be changed during the decay phase to increase the ratio of high-quality data.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about BabyLlama distillation:

## BabyLlama

BabyLlama trains an ensemble consisting of GPT-2 and a small LLaMA model on the 10M-word BabyLM dataset, and then distills this ensemble into a smaller, 58M-parameter LLaMA model. Despite its reduced size, the distilled LLaMA model not only retains the performance of the larger models, but also exceeds it.

The BabyLlama model (Timiryasov and Tastet, 2023) was among the leading solutions in the original BabyLM challenge and serves as the state-of-the-art baseline for the second BabyLM challenge.

## BabyLlama-2

BabyLlama-2 is a 345 million parameter model distillation-pretrained from two teachers on a 10 million word corpus for the BabyLM competition, and on BLiMP and SuperGLUE benchmarks, it outperforms baselines trained on both 10 and 100 million word datasets with the same data mix, as well as its teacher models. BabyLlama-2 utilizes distillation for sample-efficient pretraining, using similar-sized teacher models trained on the same limited dataset.

(arXiv 2411.06672) tested CHILDES/Gutenberg/TinyStories/Mix at 10M words across GPT2-18M..705M and found 'models trained on the CHILDES and TinyStories datasets underperformed across all model sizes' on BLiMP and EWoK — diverse Mix was best for small models; (c) BERTtime Stories (arXiv 2410.15365) mixed 50% TinyStories+generated data into the 100M-word BabyLM corpus and BLiMP DROPPED 69.2 -> 65.6-66.6 (GLUE rose), while at the 10M scale the same mix helped (BLiMP 60.6 -> 62.6). Conclusion for MythosMini: since overall = mean(BLiMP, ARC, wiki), a TinyStories-heavy pretrain would trade leaderboard points for subjective fluency. Recipe: mix 10-20% story data into the STABLE phase only, keep the WSD decay phase 100% fineweb-edu (MiniCPM evidence below), and run the standard one-feature scores.md run. Use SimpleStories (HF SimpleStories/SimpleStories: 2.14M stories, MIT license, gpt-4o-mini-generated, arXiv 2504.09184 shows better sample-efficiency than TinyStories, rich metadata incl. flesch_kincaid_grade for curriculum ordering) or roneneldan/TinyStories TinyStoriesV2 (GPT-4-only generations, ~480M GPT tokens ≈ ~2GB of bytes — equal to the entire 2B-byte budget, so no generation needed). In-domain (simple stories) Gemma-like fluency is achievable; open-domain coherence at 1M params is documented nowhere.

The only scale where heavy story data helped benchmarks was the 10M-word regime — MythosMini's 2B-token budget is past that.

Cosmopedia v2 (HuggingFaceTB/smollm-corpus, cosmopedia-v2 config: 28B tokens, 39M synthetic textbooks/stories by Mixtral, 40% generated for a middle-school audience, with audience/format metadata fields; https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceTB/smollm-corpus) contains exactly ARC-Easy-register science prose. MiniCPM (arXiv 2404.06395) documented that the WSD decay phase is the right insertion point: 'integrating high-quality labeled data in this phase presents dual advantages' and 10% decay both completes convergence and enables domain adaptation — MythosMini already uses WSD, so this is a data-swap, not a schedule change. findings.detail: Surveyed the 2024-2026 cross-tokenizer KD literature: ULD (arXiv 2402.12030, optimal-transport L1 on sorted logits, code released), Multi-Level OT (AAAI 2025), contextual dynamical mapping (arXiv 2502.11104), DSKD (arXiv 2603.22056), and — closest fit — 'Cross-Tokenizer LLM Distillation through a Byte-Level Interface' (arXiv 2604.07466: converts teacher token probs to byte-level probs, attaches a 10-projection byte decoder head, distills through it). Verdict: the byte-interface paper itself concedes 'no method, including ours, achieves consistent improvements across all benchmarks', its gains were on 2-8B LoRA students (not 1M full-pretrain), and no code is released. On top of that the capacity gap (0.6B teacher -> 1.05M student, ~600x) is far outside anything these papers tested, and BabyLlama-2 explicitly found similar-size same-data teachers work where giant teachers don't. Use the big open models for DATA instead (generation/filtering/scoring): feasibility on one 5090 is excellent — RunPod measured Qwen2-0.5B at 65,000+ tok/s under vLLM at 1024 concurrency (https://www.runpod.io/blog/rtx-5090-launch-runpod), i.e. ~230M tok/hour, so 1B tokens of bespoke synthetic text ≈ 4-6 hours with Qwen3-0.6B-class models (Gemma-3-270M faster still, quality lower). But note: TinyStoriesV2 + SimpleStories + Cosmopedia v2 (28B tokens) already exceed the entire 2B-token budget, so generation is only worth it for gaps no dataset covers (e.g., byte-level-friendly ARC-style QA pairs or ChatML-formatted simple dialogues matching data/sft.jsonl's schema).
